nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: How long did the temperature hold at 32°C before fragments were assessed for bleaching or mortality?
nodes.answer: The temperature held at 32°C until substantial bleaching or mortality was observed in approximately 50% of the fragments, which took about 5 days.
nodes.paragraph: All tanks executed the same profile and coral racks were haphazardly redistributed daily to minimize tank effects. We created a 12:12 h light:dark cycle with Radion LED aquarium lights (Ecotech Marine) with a peak midday PAR irradiance of ~ 400 mol/m2/sec. Tanks had continuous seawater input and were mixed with submersible pumps. Corals were accli- mated to indoor conditions at ~ 25 C for a week before com- mencement of a 16-day heat ramp in late February, peaking at 32 C (Fig. 1BC). Temperature was then held at 32 C until we observed substantial bleaching or mortality in ~ 50% of fragments (5 days) at which point the temperature was ramped down over 10 days to a 25 C hold. During the 32 C ramp-hold period, we removed fragments that had no viable tissue remaining (i.e., 100% tissue sloughing or complete algal overgrowth) to reduce detrimental effects on neighboring fragments. Fragments were returned to outdoor seawater tables in early May 2018 and kept in ambient flow- through conditions to allow recovery of surviving fragments (Fig. 1B).

nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What were the findings regarding the predictive value of survival after heat stress?
nodes.answer: The survival of coral samples after experiencing heat stress had strong positive predictive value for bleaching outcomes, although it also produced many false negatives.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Reef degradation induced by climate change is motivating interest in active management strategies to retain living coral cover including coral restoration. Understand- ing the level and range of heat tolerance available in coral populations is critical to determining their viability and may be important in choosing corals to propagate for restoration projects. There is a need to assess heat tolerance experimen- tally and to relate experimental performance to real-world bleaching conditions and outcomes. We sampled a model population of a key reef-building coral (Montipora capitata ) in K ne ohe Bay, O ahu, Hawai i and subjected fragments to an artificial heat stress profile. We subsequently revisited and assessed source colonies at the height of a natural bleach- ing event. Measurements of photosystem efficiency taken on samples during artificial heat stress were predictive of subsequent field bleaching responses of source colonies. By including experimental performance in additive modeling along with previous measures of symbiont community and source site characteristics, we improved predictions of later field outcomes. Survival of coral samples measured several months after experiencing the heat stress had strong positive predictive value for bleaching outcomes but also produced many false negatives.

nodes.question: What are the factors that influence heat tolerance in coral colonies?
nodes.answer: Heat tolerance in coral colonies is influenced by multiple interacting mechanisms involving the cnidarian host, intracellular symbionts, and other microbial community members, as well as thermal history and local environmental factors such as light level and water flow.
nodes.paragraph: 2017). The global prognosis for coral reefs has motivated a search for informed interventions and a deeper understanding of climate impacts, specifically on coral bleaching dynamics and heat tolerance. Within an individual coral colony, heat tolerance is a complex trait involving multiple interacting mechanisms influenced by the cnidarian host, intracellular symbionts, and other microbial community members (Carballo-Bola os et al. 2019; van Oppen and Blackall 2019). nodes.question: How can understanding heat tolerance across the holobiont contribute to coral conservation?
nodes.answer: It can help maintain diversity by expanding the selection pool when propagating corals, thus supporting conservation goals.
nodes.paragraph: Exploring intrapopulation variation in heat stress performance helps explain the full complexity of ther - mal tolerance and has practical applications such as identi- fying high-performing individuals for active management work and predicting population response for planning and setting expectations. For example, choosing coral stocks for propagation in proactive restoration projects requires knowl- edge of the heat tolerance of individuals relative to others of the same species in the same locale (Caruso et al. 2021). Any form of selection risks reducing diversity, which can be counter-productive to conservation aims especially at small effective population sizes (Baums et al. 2019). Understand- ing and detecting the partitioning of heat tolerance across the holobiont will aid in maintaining diversity by expanding the selection pool. There is growing interest in using artificial heat stress to evaluate coral performance because it allows examination of physiological and molecular responses and host symbi- ont interactions in controlled and reproducible conditions (McLachlan et al. 2020). The performance of corals during acute experimental heat treatments (measured by various metrics including visual bleaching scores, fluorometry val- ues, and chlorophyll levels) is commonly used as a proxy for thermal resilience in the wild, but this work primarily focuses on contrasting groups of corals across species, sites, and environmental gradients (van Woesik et al.

nodes.question: What was the purpose of applying artificial heat stress to coral samples in the study?
nodes.answer: The purpose was to explore the relationship between experimental and natural heat stress responses by comparing the performance of artificially heat-stressed coral fragments to their source colonies during a subsequent natural bleaching event in 2019.
nodes.paragraph: 2022; Even- sen et al. 2022; Voolstra et al. 2020; Ross Cunning et al. 2021; Palumbi et al. 2014). To the best of our knowledge, these methods have never been applied to characterize localized intrapopulation variation during actual bleaching events. Open questions remain about whether an individual coral S tolerance of artificial heat stress corresponds well to performance under natural stress events and if stress test results can be used to accurately forecast future performance. To explore the relationship between experimental and natural heat stress responses, we artificially heat-stressed sample fragments from 145 coral genotypes from a model coral population (Caruso and Rocha de Souza et al. 2022) and compared their responses to the performance of their source colonies during a subsequent natural bleaching event in 2019. We show that artificial heat stress performance cor - responds to field bleaching response of individual corals within a population and that certain evaluation metrics (Fv/ Fm decay, overall survivorship) were more effective at iden- tifying bleaching-resilient colonies, while visual health scor - ing during artificial heat stress had little predictive value.

nodes.question: What factors influence the rate and magnitude of symbiont mass expulsion in corals?
nodes.answer: The rate and magnitude of symbiont mass expulsion depend on the severity of the bleaching stressor, the coral host species and genotype, and the relative abundance and identity of the Symbiodiniaceae it hosts.
nodes.paragraph: 2020; Hoadley et al. 2019; Silverstein et al. 2017). The rate and magnitude of symbiont mass expulsion depend on the severity of the bleaching stressor, the coral host species and genotype, and the relative abundance and identity of the Symbiodiniaceae it hosts (Cunning and Baker 2013; Silverstein et al. 2017). For instance, corals hosting Durusdinium trenchii are particularly tolerant to bleaching and environmental stress (Chen et al. 2020; Silverstein et al. 2017; van Oppen et al. 2005). Indeed, many corals can shift their symbiont communities in favor of Durusdinium after exposure to bleaching, demonstrating their ability to acclimatize or adapt through symbiont recombination (Baker 2004; Claar et al. 2020). While it is well established that bleaching can drive shifts in symbiont communities, few studies have directly quantified symbiont expulsion as an ongoing regulatory (homeostatic) mechanism of coral-algal symbiosis especially in the absence of heat stress and associated dysbiosis. Previous research has demonstrated that corals routinely expel symbionts into their environment and expulsion rates can vary seasonally and in response to varying temperature and light conditions (Dimond and Carrington 2008; Hoegh-Guldberg et al.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Coral reef protection|Bleaching prevention_qna_013
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: Why is research on symbiont expulsion under non-bleaching conditions important?
nodes.answer: It is important to understand symbiont turnover, community composition, ambient environmental availability, and the plasticity of coral-algal symbiosis in the context of thermal stress and bleaching effects.
nodes.paragraph: 1987; McCloskey et al. 1996; Zhou et al. 2017; Yamashita et al. 2010). Moreover, because expelled symbiont can remain photosynthetically competent after expulsion, they can potentially be reacquired by neighboring adult corals or coral recruits (Ralph et al. 2001; Williamson et al. 2021). However, very little research has explored species-specific variation in ambient expulsion rates or temporal drivers of symbiont regulation (Cui et al. 2023; Yamashita et al. 2010). Research into symbiont expulsion under non-bleaching conditions is vital to better understand symbiont turnover, symbiont community composition, and ambient environmental availability as well as coral-algal symbiosis plasticity and can help us contextualize the effect of thermal stress and bleaching on coral-algal symbiosis. Here we developed a lab-based assay to quantify diel expulsion rates from replicate coral fragments in order to quantify, for the first time, diel patterns of symbiont expulsion under ambient conditions across a variety of Caribbean reef-building coral species. Our results offer insight into the mechanisms driving symbiont turnover and community composition and can inform future work on coral-algal symbiosis during bleaching and subsequent recovery.

nodes.question: What was measured after the corals were incubated in the chambers?
nodes.answer: Daytime expulsion was measured under lights and nighttime expulsion was measured in darkness.
nodes.paragraph: These chambers were then partially submerged in a 28 C seawater jacket under 110 mol quanta m 2 S 1 on a 12 h:12 h light dark cycle (Al Hydra 52s, Aqua Illumination, C2 Development Inc.) with daytime expulsion measured under lights and nighttime expulsion measured in darkness. On each day of observation, a randomized subset of experimental fragments were selected from adjacent 659 Coral Reefs (2025) 44:657 667 tanks with identical temperature and light conditions as the incubation water jacket. These fragments were gently rinsed with 0.2 m FSW to remove any potential symbionts adhered to the tissue surface. Once rinsed, corals were placed in each incubation chamber, with between eight and twelve chambers run in parallel. Throughout the incubation period, the chambers were agitated periodically to promote water movement. After 7 h spent in the chambers, corals were removed and carefully rinsed with 0.2 m FSW again, this time to dislodge any symbionts adhering to the coral surface into the chamber water. Pre-experiment testing using Imaging Pulse Amplitude Modulated Fluorometry (IPAM, Walz, Effeltrich, Germany) indicated that coral health (measured as Fv/Fm) was not affected by the incubation chambers indicating chamber-induced stress is negligible in expulsion.

nodes.question: How were Symbiodiniaceae expulsion rates calculated in the described study?
nodes.answer: Symbiodiniaceae expulsion rates were calculated by averaging hemocytometer counts, incorporating a loss factor for potential cell loss during centrifugation, and standardizing the expulsion rate to coral tissue surface area (cm2) per hour.
nodes.paragraph: Calculating expulsion rates For each cell pellet resuspended and preserved in Lugols, four rounds of hemocytometer counts were conducted using an inverted microscope. Symbiodiniaceae expulsion rates were calculated by averaging the counts and using the following formula: A loss factor was incorporated into calculations to account for potential cell loss during the centrifugation process. An aliquot of axenic cultured symbionts was counted using the hemocytometer at culture density, diluted to 150 mL, then run through the centrifugation process and counted again. About 33% of cells were calculated as lost in the supernatant across replicates. Expulsion was calculated in terms of cells expelled per hour and standardized to coral tissue surface area (cm2) as determined from the photographs (ImageJ). The overall expulsion rate per cm2 of tissue per hour was then calculated using the following equation: DNA extraction and qPCR DNA from coral tissue biopsies and water samples were extracted and purified from SDS archives using established protocols described in Baker and Cunning (2016). After the DNA was extracted, samples were processed using quantitative PCR (qPCR) (QuantStudio 3, Applied Biosystems, USA) to identify to the generic level which Symbiodiniaceae were present.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Coral reef protection|Bleaching prevention_qna_016
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What external conditions may lead to the persistence of cryptic juveniles after events like coral bleaching?
nodes.answer: Low coral prey availability, such as after bleaching events or COTS outbreaks, may lead to the persistence of cryptic juveniles for some time.
nodes.paragraph: Over multiple recruitment events, cohorts of juveniles have the potential to accumulate as a hidden army in the reef infrastructure until suitable condi- tions manifest, serving as a proximate source of outbreaks. In situations of low coral prey such as after bleaching events or COTS outbreaks, these cryptic juveniles may persist for some time (Byrne et al. 2023; Wolfe and Byrne 2024). A delayed switch to the adult diet and habitat occurs in other predatory sea stars, potentially influenced by density depend- ent feedback (Byrne et al. 2021; Nauen 1978). For juvenile COTS, the switch to corallivory may be influenced by inter - ference competition/semiochemicals from conspecific adults (Webb et al. 2024). The inability to target COTS across its benthic phases in mitigation/control programs emphasises the need for increased knowledge of the juvenile stage. The timing and size at which the diet shift to corallivory occurs varies among juveniles and depends on availability of preferred coral prey, as well as the risk of sublethal pre- dation/damage from coral tentacles (Deaker et al. 2021a ; Johansson et al.
